facts.title: Named After a Devil
facts.text: Nickel's name comes from the German "Kupfernickel," meaning "copper-devil" or "Old Nick's copper." Medieval Saxon miners cursed a reddish ore that looked like copper but yielded none, blaming a mischievous goblin (Nickel). The Swedish chemist Axel Fredrik Cronstedt isolated the metal from this very ore in 1751.

facts.title: It Used to Be Magnetic
facts.text: Nickel is one of only four elements that are ferromagnetic at room temperature, alongside iron, cobalt, and gadolinium. This means it can be permanently magnetized and is strongly attracted to magnets. However, if you heat nickel above its Curie temperature of about 354 degrees Celsius, it abruptly loses its magnetism.

facts.title: The Coin With Almost No Nickel
facts.text: The American five-cent coin is called a "nickel," but it is actually only 25 percent nickel and 75 percent copper. Ironically, the U.S. one-cent penny and even the silvery dime contain copper as their main metal too. Pure nickel coins were once common in countries like Canada and Switzerland.

facts.title: Stainless Steel's Secret Ingredient
facts.text: Roughly two-thirds of all nickel produced goes into making stainless steel. Adding about 8 to 10 percent nickel to chromium steel creates the most common type, called 18/8 or 304 stainless, used in kitchen sinks and cutlery. The nickel stabilizes the steel's crystal structure and dramatically boosts its resistance to corrosion.

facts.title: A Planet's Iron Heart
facts.text: Earth's core is composed mainly of an iron-nickel alloy, with nickel making up an estimated 5 to 10 percent of it. The swirling motion of this molten metal generates Earth's magnetic field, which shields us from solar radiation. Many iron meteorites are also iron-nickel alloys, and their nickel content is how scientists tell them apart from ordinary rocks.

facts.title: The Memory Metal
facts.text: Nitinol, an alloy of nickel and titanium, is a remarkable "shape-memory" material. Bend it out of shape, then warm it up, and it springs back to its original form as if it remembered. This property makes Nitinol invaluable for medical stents that expand inside arteries and for bendable, hard-to-break eyeglass frames.

facts.title: Powering Your Devices
facts.text: Nickel is a key component of rechargeable batteries, including nickel-cadmium (NiCd) and nickel-metal-hydride (NiMH) cells. It is also vital in the lithium-ion batteries that power electric cars, where high-nickel cathodes pack in more energy. This battery demand is now one of the fastest-growing reasons the world mines nickel.

facts.title: A Common Allergy Culprit
facts.text: Nickel is the single most common cause of allergic contact dermatitis, affecting an estimated 10 to 20 percent of people. The reaction often appears as an itchy rash where jewelry, watch backs, or belt buckles touch the skin. To protect consumers, the European Union strictly limits how much nickel can leach from items worn against the body.

facts.title: Essential Element of Life
facts.text: Many bacteria, archaea, plants, and fungi depend on nickel as a trace nutrient. It sits at the heart of at least nine known enzymes, including urease, which breaks down urea, and the hydrogenases that handle hydrogen gas. Plants like soybeans need tiny amounts of nickel to grow properly, making it a genuine micronutrient.

facts.title: The Mond Purification Trick
facts.text: In 1890, chemist Ludwig Mond discovered that nickel reacts with carbon monoxide gas at around 50 degrees Celsius to form a volatile compound called nickel tetracarbonyl. Heated further, this gas decomposes and deposits pure nickel back out. This elegant "Mond process" is still used industrially to refine nickel to extreme purity, though the gas is dangerously toxic.
